answers.subject: Competitive bidding; aggregation of orders
answers.input: A department anticipates purchasing laboratory consumables from a single supplier under a series of purchase orders during the fiscal year. Each order is expected to fall between $20,000 and $30,000. Aggregate expenditure with the supplier for the year is projected at approximately $140,000. No strategically sourced agreement covers the items. Whether the requirement to competitively bid is determined by the aggregate annual expenditure with the supplier rather than by the value of each order, and whether the department may continue to issue individual orders without a competitive solicitation.
answers.answer:
Answer: No, competitive bid is required because the aggregate annual expenditure of $140,000 exceeds the $100,000 threshold [1], and individual orders may not be issued without a competitive solicitation.
Rule: Competitive bid required: YES ($140,000; threshold $100,000). SSPR required: YES (threshold $100,000; sections I, VII, VIII).
Source: BFB-BUS-43: Purchases of Goods and Services; Supply Chain Management (Interim, issued/effective January 26, 2026), p.9, III, C. Expenditures of $100,000 or More Annually, 1. General Requirements: "requires that UC competitively bid all purchases with proposed annual expenditure of $100,000 or more unless an exception applies"; Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR) (Revised 12-2025), p.1, header: "Non-Federal purchases ≥$100,000"
Conditions: The department must comply with competitive bidding requirements for the aggregate amount of $140,000 [1], and the SSPR form (sections I, VII, VIII) is required [2].
cited: BFB-BUS-43: Procurement & Supply Chain Management (Interim, Jan 2026) p.21
Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR, Rev. 12-2025) p.1

answers.subject: Small Business First; federally funded purchase
answers.input: A department proposes to purchase an instrument at a cost of $180,000, funded entirely by a National Science Foundation grant. A certified small business is able to supply the instrument, and the department has obtained one quotation from it. Whether the Small Business First provisions permit award to the certified small business without a competitive solicitation at this value, and whether the federal source of funds alters the number of quotations required or the sections of the SSPR to be completed.
answers.answer:
Answer: Yes, the Small Business First provisions permit award to the certified small business without a competitive solicitation at this value. The federal source of funds does not alter the number of quotations required, which is two, and the sections of the SSPR to be completed are III, VII, and VIII.
Rule: Competitive bid required: NO ($180,000; threshold $100,000; exemption: certified small business / DVBE (under $250,000)). SSPR required: YES (threshold $50,000; sections I, III, VII, VIII). Also required: Federal Funds Checklist; Anti-Lobbying Verification (Byrd Amendment); Debarment & Suspension Verification; Uniform Guidance (2 CFR 200) Flow-Down Articles.
Source: BFB-BUS-43: Purchases of Goods and Services; Supply Chain Management (Interim, issued/effective January 26, 2026), p.9, III, C. Expenditures of $100,000 or More Annually, 1. General Requirements: "requires that UC competitively bid all purchases with proposed annual expenditure of $100,000 or more unless an exception applies"; Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR) (Revised 12-2025), p.1, header: "Federal Grant/Cooperative Agreement purchases ≥$50,000"; FAR 2.101 Definitions (inflation adjustment, 90 FR 41872) (effective October 1, 2025), Simplified acquisition threshold: "Simplified acquisition threshold means $350,000"; Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR) (Revised 12-2025), p.1, I. Source Selection, Non-Federal Funds: "Certified Small Business or DVBE (Only <$250k; Complete III, VII, VIII)"; BFB-BUS-43: Purchases of Goods and Services; Supply Chain Management (Interim, issued/effective January 26, 2026), p.25, III, Part 3, C. Small Business First: "award purchase agreements valued up to $250,000 to a certified Small Business"; BFB-BUS-43: Purchases of Goods and Services; Supply Chain Management (Interim, issued/effective January 26, 2026), p.25, III, Part 3, C. Small Business First, 1. General Requirements (a)-(b): "If the goods and/or services are valued greater than $100,000 but less than $250,000 annually, UC must obtain at least two (2) quotes"; Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR) (Revised 12-2025), p.1, I. Source Selection, Federal Funds: "Certified Small Business (Only <$100K; Complete III, VII, VIII)"; UC Procurement Federal Funds Checklist (Rev. 11.2025 (file dated 12/15/25)), Required documentation table: "Anti-Lobby Verification ≥ $100,000"
Conditions: The SSPR form must include sections III, VII, and VIII [1], and two quotes must be obtained from certified small businesses/DVBEs [4]. Federal funds require the SSPR form to be completed for purchases ≥$50,000 [2].
cited: BFB-BUS-43: Procurement & Supply Chain Management (Interim, Jan 2026) p.25
Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form p.
BFB-BUS-43: Procurement & Supply Chain Management (Interim, Jan 2026) p.25

answers.subject: Mixed funding; SSPR federal threshold
answers.input: A department proposes a purchase of $120,000, of which $50,000 is charged to a federal grant and $70,000 to departmental funds. Whether the federal portion of the purchase meets the SSPR threshold for federally funded grant purchases such that the federal requirements apply to the entire transaction, and which side of the SSPR form is to be completed.
answers.answer:
Answer: Yes, the federal portion of the purchase meets the SSPR threshold for federally funded grant purchases, and the Federal side of the SSPR form is to be completed.
Rule: Federal rules apply to the entire transaction (federal portion $50,000 meets the $50,000 federal grant threshold). Competitive bid required: YES ($120,000; threshold $100,000). SSPR required: YES (threshold $50,000; sections I, VII, VIII). Also required: Federal Funds Checklist; Anti-Lobbying Verification (Byrd Amendment); Debarment & Suspension Verification; Uniform Guidance (2 CFR 200) Flow-Down Articles.
Source: Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR) (Revised 12-2025), p.1, I. Source Selection (Required): "where the federal portion exceeds the above thresholds, check Federal side only"; BFB-BUS-43: Purchases of Goods and Services; Supply Chain Management (Interim, issued/effective January 26, 2026), p.9, III, C. Expenditures of $100,000 or More Annually, 1. General Requirements: "requires that UC competitively bid all purchases with proposed annual expenditure of $100,000 or more unless an exception applies"; Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR) (Revised 12-2025), p.1, header: "Federal Grant/Cooperative Agreement purchases ≥$50,000"; FAR 2.101 Definitions (inflation adjustment, 90 FR 41872) (effective October 1, 2025), Simplified acquisition threshold: "Simplified acquisition threshold means $350,000"; UC Procurement Federal Funds Checklist (Rev. 11.2025 (file dated 12/15/25)), Required documentation table: "Anti-Lobby Verification ≥ $100,000"
Conditions: The federal portion exceeds the $50,000 SSPR threshold for federal grant purchases [1], and federal requirements apply to the entire transaction because the federal portion meets the $50,000 threshold [1]. The Federal side of the SSPR form must be completed [1].
cited: Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form p.

answers.subject: Mixed funding; status of the SSPR FAQ
answers.input: The SSPR FAQ states that where the federal portion of a mixed-funded transaction exceeds $10,000, federal requirements apply to the whole transaction. The current SSPR form (Rev. 12-2025) instructs that for mixed funding the federal side is to be completed where the federal portion exceeds the thresholds stated on the form ($15,000 for contracts; $50,000 for grants and cooperative agreements). Whether the $10,000 federal-portion rule stated in the FAQ remains operative, or has been superseded by the thresholds stated on the Rev. 12-2025 form.
answers.answer:
Answer: No, the $10,000 federal-portion rule stated in the FAQ is superseded by the thresholds stated on the Rev. 12-2025 form [7].
Rule: Competitive bid required: NO ($50,000; threshold $100,000). SSPR required: YES (threshold $50,000; sections I, II, VII, VIII). Also required: Federal Funds Checklist; Debarment & Suspension Verification; Uniform Guidance (2 CFR 200) Flow-Down Articles.
Source: BFB-BUS-43: Purchases of Goods and Services; Supply Chain Management (Interim, issued/effective January 26, 2026), p.9, III, C. Expenditures of $100,000 or More Annually, 1. General Requirements: "requires that UC competitively bid all purchases with proposed annual expenditure of $100,000 or more unless an exception applies"; Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR) (Revised 12-2025), p.1, header: "Federal Grant/Cooperative Agreement purchases ≥$50,000"; FAR 2.101 Definitions (inflation adjustment, 90 FR 41872) (effective October 1, 2025), Simplified acquisition threshold: "Simplified acquisition threshold means $350,000"
Conditions: For mixed funding, the federal side of the SSPR form must be completed where the federal portion exceeds the thresholds stated on the form ($15,000 for contracts; $50,000 for grants and cooperative agreements) [7].
cited: Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR, Rev. 12-2025) p.1

answers.subject: Former employee; participation in supplier selection
answers.input: An employee who served on the evaluation committee for a software request for proposals separated from the University eight months ago and has since formed a consulting firm. The department that issued the RFP proposes to engage the firm to implement the software selected under it. The engagement would be funded from a private gift. Whether the University may contract with the former employee's firm, and whether the source of funds bears on the answer.
answers.answer:
Answer: No, the University may not contract with the former employee's firm. The two-year ban applies because the former employee participated in the negotiations, planning, or decision-making for the contract while employed [7].
Rule: PROHIBITED for two years after leaving: the former employee took part in the negotiations, planning or decision-making for this contract while at UC (Public Contract Code; OGC post-employment rules 3(a)).
Source: Summary of the Post-Employment Rules (UC Office of the General Counsel) (October 2023), p.3, 3(a) Public Contract Code - Restrictions on Providing Goods or Services: "You are barred for two years from entering into a contract with the University to provide goods or services, if you engaged in any negotiations, planning, arrangements, or any part of the decision-making process related to the contract while still employed by the University."; Summary of the Post-Employment Rules (UC Office of the General Counsel) (October 2023), p.3, 3(b) Public Contract Code - Restrictions on Providing Goods or Services: "You are barred for 12 months after leaving the University from entering into a contract with the University department you formerly worked for, if you were employed by that department in a policymaking position in the same general subject area as the proposed contract."; Summary of the Post-Employment Rules (UC Office of the General Counsel) (October 2023), p.3, 3(a)/3(b) note: "retirees are generally exempt from this ban and may nonetheless be hired back by the University"; Summary of the Post-Employment Rules (UC Office of the General Counsel) (October 2023), p.3, 2. One Year Ban on Representing Other Parties Before the University: "You are barred for one year after leaving the University from appearing before or communicating with your campus while representing another person, in an attempt to influence certain University proceedings if you are being paid to do so."
Conditions: The source of funds (private gift) does not affect the applicability of the ban [7]. The former employee's role on the evaluation committee constitutes participation in the decision-making process, triggering the two-year prohibition [7]. Retirees are generally exempt, but this case does not indicate retirement [7].
cited: BFB-BUS-43: Procurement & Supply Chain Management (Interim, Jan 2026) p.28

answers.subject: Former employee; policy-making position; retiree
answers.input: A department director retired from the University six months ago. Her former department proposes to retain her as an independent contractor to advise on a procurement in the subject area she managed while employed. She had no involvement in planning the procurement before her retirement. Whether the twelve-month restriction applicable to former employees who held policy-making responsibilities applies to a retiree, and how the retiree exemption described in the Office of the General Counsel summary is to be reconciled with BUS-43 Part III.F.2.b.
answers.answer:
Answer: No, the twelve-month restriction does not apply to a retiree who is proposed to be retained as an independent contractor for advice in a subject area she previously managed, as retirees are generally exempt from this ban [7].
Rule: Retirees are generally exempt from the two-year and 12-month contracting bans and may be hired back by the University; confirm with the campus conflict-of-interest office.
Source: Summary of the Post-Employment Rules (UC Office of the General Counsel) (October 2023), p.3, 3(a) Public Contract Code - Restrictions on Providing Goods or Services: "You are barred for two years from entering into a contract with the University to provide goods or services, if you engaged in any negotiations, planning, arrangements, or any part of the decision-making process related to the contract while still employed by the University."; Summary of the Post-Employment Rules (UC Office of the General Counsel) (October 2023), p.3, 3(b) Public Contract Code - Restrictions on Providing Goods or Services: "You are barred for 12 months after leaving the University from entering into a contract with the University department you formerly worked for, if you were employed by that department in a policymaking position in the same general subject area as the proposed contract."; Summary of the Post-Employment Rules (UC Office of the General Counsel) (October 2023), p.3, 3(a)/3(b) note: "retirees are generally exempt from this ban and may nonetheless be hired back by the University"; Summary of the Post-Employment Rules (UC Office of the General Counsel) (October 2023), p.3, 2. One Year Ban on Representing Other Parties Before the University: "You are barred for one year after leaving the University from appearing before or communicating with your campus while representing another person, in an attempt to influence certain University proceedings if you are being paid to do so."
Conditions: Retirees are exempt from the twelve-month restriction if they are retained as independent contractors and had no involvement in planning the procurement before retirement [7]. The retiree exemption described in the Office of the General Counsel summary reconciles with BUS-43 Part III.F.2.b by allowing retirees to be hired back or contracted for services, provided they did not participate in the decision-making process for the procurement [1].
cited: BFB-BUS-43: Procurement & Supply Chain Management (Interim, Jan 2026) p.28
Post-Employment Conflict of Interest Rules p.3

answers.subject: Former employee; asserted one-year contracting ban
answers.input: A department states that a former employee 'is subject to a one-year contract ban' and asks whether it may engage him as an independent contractor, for a project funded by a federal award, once the year has elapsed. The department has not identified the former employee's role or the date of separation. Whether University policy imposes a one-year ban on contracting with former employees as described, and if not, which post-employment restrictions govern the proposed engagement and what facts are required to apply them.
answers.answer:
Answer: No, University policy does not impose a one-year ban on contracting with former employees as described. The one-year ban applies to representing another party before the University for pay, not to contracting as an independent contractor.
Rule: No contracting ban is triggered on the facts given, but check both bans before contracting: two years if the former employee took part in the decision-making for this contract, 12 months if they held a policymaking position in the contracting department; retirees are generally exempt. The project's funding source is irrelevant.
Source: FAR 2.101 Definitions (inflation adjustment, 90 FR 41872) (effective October 1, 2025), Micro-purchase threshold: "Micro-purchase threshold means $15,000"; BFB-BUS-43: Purchases of Goods and Services; Supply Chain Management (Interim, issued/effective January 26, 2026), p.9, III, B. Expenditure of Less Than $100,000 Annually, 4. Micro-purchase Award: "may establish a micro-purchase threshold of up to $50,000 in accordance with the OMB"; Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR) (Revised 12-2025), p.1, footnote *: "Campus locations may establish a micro-purchase threshold of up to $50,000 for grants and cooperative agreements"; FAR 2.101 Definitions (inflation adjustment, 90 FR 41872) (effective October 1, 2025), Simplified acquisition threshold: "Simplified acquisition threshold means $350,000"; UC Procurement Federal Funds Checklist (Rev. 11.2025 (file dated 12/15/25)), Required documentation table: "Anti-Lobby Verification ≥ $100,000"; Summary of the Post-Employment Rules (UC Office of the General Counsel) (October 2023), p.3, 3(a) Public Contract Code - Restrictions on Providing Goods or Services: "You are barred for two years from entering into a contract with the University to provide goods or services, if you engaged in any negotiations, planning, arrangements, or any part of the decision-making process related to the contract while still employed by the University."; Summary of the Post-Employment Rules (UC Office of the General Counsel) (October 2023), p.3, 3(b) Public Contract Code - Restrictions on Providing Goods or Services: "You are barred for 12 months after leaving the University from entering into a contract with the University department you formerly worked for, if you were employed by that department in a policymaking position in the same general subject area as the proposed contract."; Summary of the Post-Employment Rules (UC Office of the General Counsel) (October 2023), p.3, 3(a)/3(b) note: "retirees are generally exempt from this ban and may nonetheless be hired back by the University"; Summary of the Post-Employment Rules (UC Office of the General Counsel) (October 2023), p.3, 2. One Year Ban on Representing Other Parties Before the University: "You are barred for one year after leaving the University from appearing before or communicating with your campus while representing another person, in an attempt to influence certain University proceedings if you are being paid to do so."
Conditions: The department must determine the former employee's prior role and date of separation to apply the two-year or 12-month ban, or confirm if the employee is a retiree [1], [5]. For independent contractor status, review the UC Independent Contractor Guidelines to ensure the individual is not subject to employee classifications [4].
cited: Post-Employment Conflict of Interest Rules p.15
UC Independent Contractor Guidelines p.10

answers.subject: Contracting out; covered services; new facility
answers.input: A campus unit proposes a three-year contract, valued at $450,000, with an outside firm to provide custodial services in a newly acquired building. No University custodial staff are presently assigned to the building, and the unit represents that no University position would be eliminated. Whether the proposed contract is permitted under Regents Policy 5402; whether advance notice to AFSCME 3299 is required; and whether the wage and benefit parity provisions apply to the contract.
answers.answer:
Answer: No, the proposed contract is not permitted under Regents Policy 5402 because custodial services are a covered service and contracting out is prohibited unless an exception applies. Advance notice to AFSCME 3299 is required because the contract exceeds $100,000. Wage and benefit parity provisions apply to the contract because it exceeds $100,000 and is for a term longer than 90 days [1], [3], [5].
Rule: Competitive bid required: YES ($150,000; threshold $100,000). SSPR required: YES (threshold $100,000; sections I, VII, VIII). Covered service (custodial) under Regents Policy 5402: allowed only under a listed exception. AFSCME notice: YES. Wage/benefit parity: YES.
Source: BFB-BUS-43: Purchases of Goods and Services; Supply Chain Management (Interim, issued/effective January 26, 2026), p.9, III, C. Expenditures of $100,000 or More Annually, 1. General Requirements: "requires that UC competitively bid all purchases with proposed annual expenditure of $100,000 or more unless an exception applies"; Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR) (Revised 12-2025), p.1, header: "Non-Federal purchases ≥$100,000"; Regents Policy 5402: Policy Generally Prohibiting Contracting for Services (Approved November 14, 2019; amended January 23, 2020), p.1, Policy Summary: "There shall be a general prohibition on contracting out for services and functions that can be performed by University staff"; AFSCME 3299 Article 5: Contracting Out (1-31-20), p.3, D. Notice Provisions, 1: "The University shall provide notice to AFSCME 3299 prior to entering into, extending or renewing a contract that includes Covered Services valued at over $100,000"; Regents Policy 5402: Policy Generally Prohibiting Contracting for Services (Approved November 14, 2019; amended January 23, 2020), p.3, C. Employment Standards, 1. Wage and Benefits Parity: "Contracts for covered services exceeding $100,000 and ninety (90) days' duration shall include provisions requiring the contractor"
Conditions: The contract is prohibited unless one of the listed exceptions in Regents Policy 5402 applies, such as the services are incidental to a property lease [6]. AFSCME 3299 must be notified at least 30 calendar days prior to entering, extending, or renewing the contract [3]. The contractor must provide wages and benefits equivalent to UC employees performing the same work [5].
cited: Regents Policy 5402: Policy Generally Prohibiting Contracting for Services p.3
Article 5: Contracting Out p.3

answers.subject: Contracting out; temporary absence of staff
answers.input: A clinical department proposes to contract for medical imaging technician services for six months, at a cost of $90,000, while two University technicians are on approved leave. Whether the temporary absence of University staff is a recognized basis for contracting out a covered service, and whether notice to AFSCME 3299 is required at the stated value.
answers.answer:
Answer: No, notice to AFSCME 3299 is not required at the stated value of $90,000.
Rule: Competitive bid required: NO ($90,000; threshold $100,000). SSPR required: NO (threshold $100,000). Covered service (medical imaging) under Regents Policy 5402: allowed only under a listed exception. AFSCME notice: NO.
Source: BFB-BUS-43: Purchases of Goods and Services; Supply Chain Management (Interim, issued/effective January 26, 2026), p.9, III, C. Expenditures of $100,000 or More Annually, 1. General Requirements: "requires that UC competitively bid all purchases with proposed annual expenditure of $100,000 or more unless an exception applies"; Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR) (Revised 12-2025), p.1, header: "Non-Federal purchases ≥$100,000"; Regents Policy 5402: Policy Generally Prohibiting Contracting for Services (Approved November 14, 2019; amended January 23, 2020), p.1, Policy Summary: "There shall be a general prohibition on contracting out for services and functions that can be performed by University staff"; AFSCME 3299 Article 5: Contracting Out (1-31-20), p.3, D. Notice Provisions, 1: "The University shall provide notice to AFSCME 3299 prior to entering into, extending or renewing a contract that includes Covered Services valued at over $100,000"
Conditions: The temporary absence of University staff may be a recognized basis for contracting out a covered service under the exception for short-term staffing needs [7]. However, since the total value is below $100,000, AFSCME 3299 notice is not required [3].
cited: Article 5: Contracting Out p.3
Article 5: Contracting Out p.3

answers.subject: Equipment; inventorial threshold; subsequent accessory
answers.input: A department purchased a microscope in March at a cost of $4,800. In June it purchased an objective lens for the same microscope at a cost of $1,400. The combined cost is $6,200. Whether the microscope, the lens, or the combined asset must be inventoried and tagged under BUS-29.
answers.answer:
Answer: No, the microscope and the objective lens do not need to be inventoried and tagged individually as they are below the $5,000 threshold for inventorial equipment [1], [2]. However, the combined cost of $6,200 exceeds the threshold, but since they are not considered inventorial equipment under BUS-29, they still do not require tagging [1], [2].
Rule: Item 1 ($4,800): no tagging required (BUS-29 threshold $5,000). Item 2 ($1,400): no tagging required (BUS-29 threshold $5,000). Item 3 ($6,200): must be tagged (BUS-29 threshold $5,000).
Source: BFB-BUS-29: Management and Control of University Equipment (UC-FA-21-0555 (accessible)), p.3, II. Definitions, Non-Inventorial Equipment: "NON-INVENTORIAL EQUIPMENT: Equipment which is non-expendable, tangible, personal property acquired for less than $5,000"
Conditions: None.
cited: BFB-BUS-29: Management & Control of University Equipment p.8
BFB-BUS-29: Management & Control of University Equipment p.8

answers.subject: Sole source; brand preference
answers.input: A principal investigator requests sole-source award of a $140,000 purchase of a sequencing instrument of a particular manufacturer, on the ground that the laboratory's protocols were developed on that manufacturer's platform. Two other manufacturers offer instruments meeting the stated technical specifications. Whether the stated ground constitutes a permissible sole source justification, and if not, what procurement method is required at this value.
answers.answer:
Answer: No, the stated ground does not constitute a permissible sole source justification. Competitive bid is not required, but SSPR form is required with justification in Section IV.
Rule: Competitive bid required: NO ($140,000; threshold $100,000; exemption: sole source (with allowable SSPR Section IV justification)). SSPR required: YES (threshold $100,000; sections I, III, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII).
Source: BFB-BUS-43: Purchases of Goods and Services; Supply Chain Management (Interim, issued/effective January 26, 2026), p.9, III, C. Expenditures of $100,000 or More Annually, 1. General Requirements: "requires that UC competitively bid all purchases with proposed annual expenditure of $100,000 or more unless an exception applies"; Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR) (Revised 12-2025), p.1, header: "Non-Federal purchases ≥$100,000"
Conditions: Sole source must be documented with an allowable justification in SSPR Section IV: One-of-a-kind/Unique, Match existing (list UC PO#). Price, brand name, and pre-work with the supplier that excludes competition are NOT allowable [1]. SSPR sections I, III, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII are required [2].
cited: Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR, Rev. 12-2025) p.2
Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form p.

answers.subject: Emergency purchase; exception to competitive bidding
answers.input: A water main failure has flooded a research laboratory. The department requires a restoration contractor immediately. The estimated cost is $160,000. Whether an emergency exception to the competitive bidding requirement is available; by whom it may be granted; and what the department must document.
answers.answer:
Answer: Yes, an emergency exception to the competitive bidding requirement is available for this $160,000 restoration project due to the unusual & compelling urgency caused by the water main failure.
Rule: Competitive bid required: NO ($160,000; threshold $100,000; exemption: unusual & compelling urgency (non-federal only)). SSPR required: YES (threshold $100,000; sections I, VI, VII, VIII).
Source: BFB-BUS-43: Purchases of Goods and Services; Supply Chain Management (Interim, issued/effective January 26, 2026), p.9, III, C. Expenditures of $100,000 or More Annually, 1. General Requirements: "requires that UC competitively bid all purchases with proposed annual expenditure of $100,000 or more unless an exception applies"; Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR) (Revised 12-2025), p.1, header: "Non-Federal purchases ≥$100,000"
Conditions: The department must document the emergency situation, including the water main failure and the immediate need for restoration, as per UC Independent Contractor Guidelines [6]. The exemption applies only to non-federal purchases and must be justified as an emergency to prevent stoppage of University operations [6]. SSPR form is still required [1].
cited: UC Terms and Conditions of Purchase (April 2025) p.10
Article 5: Contracting Out p.2

answers.subject: Business meals; required documentation
answers.input: A department submits an Entertainment Check Request for a working lunch held with a visiting academic delegation. The request states the date, the name of the restaurant and the total charged, and attaches an itemized receipt for $412. No other information is provided. Whether the request is complete for purposes of BUS-79, and if not, what information must be supplied before it may be approved.
answers.answer:
Answer: No, the request is not complete. The request must include the type of expense, type of event, number of participants with a guest list, date and location, business-related purpose, and the signature of the approving authority and host. Additionally, the receipt must include the names and titles of all participants to establish the business-related relationship [1].
Rule: Documentation required for a business meal or entertainment expense (BUS-79): type of expense; type of event; number of participants with a guest list giving each participant's name, title and occupation or group affiliation; date and location; the business-related purpose of the occasion; and the signature, printed name and department of the approving authority (plus the host's signature for entertainment, recruitment and morale-building events). Expenses of $75 or more per occasion need original itemized receipts.
Source: BFB-BUS-79: Expenditures for Business Meetings, Entertainment, and Other Occasions (UC-FA-22-0617 (updated 12.15.2022, accessible)), p.17, IV.B.1 Reimbursement or Payment Request: "The completed request must include the following information:"; BFB-BUS-79: Expenditures for Business Meetings, Entertainment, and Other Occasions (UC-FA-22-0617 (updated 12.15.2022, accessible)), p.17, IV.B.1 Reimbursement or Payment Request: "Type of expense (lunch, dinner, etc.);"; BFB-BUS-79: Expenditures for Business Meetings, Entertainment, and Other Occasions (UC-FA-22-0617 (updated 12.15.2022, accessible)), p.17, IV.B.1 Reimbursement or Payment Request: "Type of event;"; BFB-BUS-79: Expenditures for Business Meetings, Entertainment, and Other Occasions (UC-FA-22-0617 (updated 12.15.2022, accessible)), p.17, IV.B.1 Reimbursement or Payment Request: "Number of participants (attach a guest list containing the name and title of participants, and their occupation or group affiliation, in order to establish the business-related relationship to the University)"; BFB-BUS-79: Expenditures for Business Meetings, Entertainment, and Other Occasions (UC-FA-22-0617 (updated 12.15.2022, accessible)), p.17, IV.B.1 Reimbursement or Payment Request: "Date and location of the event;"; BFB-BUS-79: Expenditures for Business Meetings, Entertainment, and Other Occasions (UC-FA-22-0617 (updated 12.15.2022, accessible)), p.17, IV.B.1 Reimbursement or Payment Request: "Business-related nature of the occasion or purpose of the event; and"; BFB-BUS-79: Expenditures for Business Meetings, Entertainment, and Other Occasions (UC-FA-22-0617 (updated 12.15.2022, accessible)), p.17, IV.B.1 Reimbursement or Payment Request: "The signature, printed name, and department of the department head or approving authority."; answers.subject: Tax-free alcohol; asserted authority of a DEA registration
answers.input: A laboratory holds a Drug Enforcement Administration registration for controlled substances. It asks to purchase 200-proof ethanol free of tax 'under its DEA registration.' Whether a DEA registration authorizes the purchase of tax-free alcohol, and what authorization is in fact required before a supplier may ship.
answers.answer:
Answer: No, a DEA registration does not authorize the purchase of tax-free alcohol. Authorization is obtained through the University's TTB permit.
Rule: Tax-free alcohol is bought under the University's TTB permit, held in the name of The Regents: the vendor must have a signed copy of the valid permit on file, inventories are semiannual, and receipts and records are kept for every delivery.
Source: BFB-BUS-2 / UCPS 120031: Tax-Free Alcohol Permits, Records, and Operations (Issued 6/30/2012), p.2, III.A Securing Industrial Use Permits: "Applications for industrial use permits for tax-free alcohol are filed with the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau of the U.S. Department of the Treasury"; BFB-BUS-2 / UCPS 120031: Tax-Free Alcohol Permits, Records, and Operations (Issued 6/30/2012), p.2, III.A Securing Industrial Use Permits: "All tax-free alcohol use applications are to be made in the name of "The Regents of the University of California.""; BFB-BUS-2 / UCPS 120031: Tax-Free Alcohol Permits, Records, and Operations (Issued 6/30/2012), p.2, III.B Approval by TTB: "TTB will issue an official numbered"; BFB-BUS-2 / UCPS 120031: Tax-Free Alcohol Permits, Records, and Operations (Issued 6/30/2012), p.2, III.B Approval by TTB: "Permits are continuous unless automatically terminated by the terms of the permit."; BFB-BUS-2 / UCPS 120031: Tax-Free Alcohol Permits, Records, and Operations (Issued 6/30/2012), p.3, III.C.1 Purchasing Requirements: "Shipments may not be made until the vendor has a signed copy of a valid permit on file"; BFB-BUS-2 / UCPS 120031: Tax-Free Alcohol Permits, Records, and Operations (Issued 6/30/2012), p.6, 5. Inventories: "a physical inventory of tax-free alcohol shall be taken semiannually or at other inventory periods approximately six months apart"; BFB-BUS-2 / UCPS 120031: Tax-Free Alcohol Permits, Records, and Operations (Issued 6/30/2012), p.5, 2. Conditions of Use of Tax-Free Alcohol: "shall sign a receipt for each delivery and shall maintain complete, accurate, and up-to-date records of all tax-free alcohol received and issued"; BFB-BUS-2 / UCPS 120031: Tax-Free Alcohol Permits, Records, and Operations (Issued 6/30/2012), p.3, III.C.2 Conditions of Use: "shall be used only on the premises of the University"
Conditions: The vendor must have a signed copy of the valid TTB permit on file [3], inventories are semiannual [6], and receipts and records are kept for every delivery [5]. Tax-free alcohol is used only on University premises [8].

answers.subject: Tax-free alcohol; physical inventory
answers.input: A department last took a physical inventory of its tax-free alcohol nine months ago. It proposes to withdraw additional alcohol from inventory this week. Whether the department is in compliance with the inventory requirement, and whether withdrawals may be made before a physical inventory is taken.
answers.answer:
Answer: No, the department is not in compliance with the inventory requirement, and withdrawals may not be made before a physical inventory is taken.
Rule: Tax-free alcohol is bought under the University's TTB permit, held in the name of The Regents: the vendor must have a signed copy of the valid permit on file, inventories are semiannual, and receipts and records are kept for every delivery.

Inventories: "a physical inventory of tax-free alcohol shall be taken semiannually or at other inventory periods approximately six months apart"; BFB-BUS-2 / UCPS 120031: Tax-Free Alcohol Permits, Records, and Operations (Issued 6/30/2012), p.5, 2. Conditions of Use of Tax-Free Alcohol: "shall sign a receipt for each delivery and shall maintain complete, accurate, and up-to-date records of all tax-free alcohol received and issued"; BFB-BUS-2 / UCPS 120031: Tax-Free Alcohol Permits, Records, and Operations (Issued 6/30/2012), p.3, III.C.2 Conditions of Use: "shall be used only on the premises of the University"
Conditions: The inventory must be taken semiannually, approximately six months apart [1], and the last inventory was nine months ago, which is beyond the allowed period. Withdrawals are permitted only if the last inventory was within six months [2].

answers.subject: Certificate of insurance; moderate digital risk
answers.input: A software-as-a-service supplier will host departmental scheduling data classified at Protection Level P2. The engagement presents no other risk exposure identified in the Risk Matrix. Whether a certificate of insurance must be collected from the supplier, and what the agreement must provide with respect to insurance.
answers.answer:
Answer: No, a Certificate of Insurance does not need to be collected, but the agreement must require the contractor to provide one on request.
Rule: Moderate risk under the BUS-63 Risk Matrix (digital risk - moderate): a Certificate of Insurance does not need to be collected, but the agreement must require the contractor to provide one on request.
Source: Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR) (Revised 12-2025), p.1, I. Source Selection (Required): "where the federal portion exceeds the above thresholds, check Federal side only"; UC BUS-63 Risk Matrix (Revised 9.19.2025), p.1, How to Use: "If the contract involves any one of the Risk Exposures C-K, the entire contract is classified as presenting High risk and a COI must be collected."; UC BUS-63 Risk Matrix (Revised 9.19.2025), p.2, High Risk: "Collection of a Certificate of Insurance (COI) is required."; UC BUS-63 Risk Matrix (Revised 9.19.2025), p.2, Low Risk / Moderate Risk: "A Certificate of Insurance (COI) does not need to be collected; the agreement or PO should require the Contractor/External Party to provide a COI to UC upon UC"
Conditions: The engagement involves digital risk with data classified at Protection Level P2, which is considered moderate risk under the BUS-63 Risk Matrix [3]. Since there are no other risk exposures identified, the contract is classified as Moderate risk, and thus a Certificate of Insurance does not need to be collected, but the agreement must require the contractor to provide one on request [3].
cited: BUS-63: Risk Matrix p.1

answers.subject: Certificate of insurance; transportation of students
answers.input: A charter bus company will transport University students to a field site under a contract valued at $18,000. Whether a certificate of insurance must be collected notwithstanding the contract value, and what minimum automobile liability limits apply.
answers.answer:
Answer: Yes, a certificate of insurance must be collected because the contract involves transportation (K. Transportation) which is a high-risk exposure under the BUS-63 Risk Matrix [1].
Rule: Competitive bid required: NO ($18,000; threshold $100,000). SSPR required: NO (threshold $100,000). High risk under the BUS-63 Risk Matrix (K. Transportation): a Certificate of Insurance must be collected before the contract is executed.
Source: BFB-BUS-43: Purchases of Goods and Services; Supply Chain Management (Interim, issued/effective January 26, 2026), p.9, III, C. Expenditures of $100,000 or More Annually, 1. General Requirements: "requires that UC competitively bid all purchases with proposed annual expenditure of $100,000 or more unless an exception applies"; Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR) (Revised 12-2025), p.1, header: "Non-Federal purchases ≥$100,000"; UC BUS-63 Risk Matrix (Revised 9.19.2025), p.1, How to Use: "If the contract involves any one of the Risk Exposures C-K, the entire contract is classified as presenting High risk and a COI must be collected."; UC BUS-63 Risk Matrix (Revised 9.19.2025), p.2, High Risk: "Collection of a Certificate of Insurance (COI) is required."; UC BUS-63 Risk Matrix (Revised 9.19.2025), p.2, Low Risk / Moderate Risk: "A Certificate of Insurance (COI) does not need to be collected; the agreement or PO should require the Contractor/External Party to provide a COI to UC upon UC"
Conditions: The minimum automobile liability limits are determined by the UC Terms and Conditions of Purchase (insurance article) and must be met by the contractor. The contractor must provide a Certificate of Insurance showing compliance with these limits prior to commencing services [6].

answers.subject: General liability limits; asserted dependence on contract value
answers.input: A caterer engaged for a department reception carries commercial general liability insurance with a per-occurrence limit of $500,000. The department takes the position that a lower limit is acceptable because the contract value is under $10,000. Whether the minimum general liability limits in the UC Terms and Conditions vary with the value of the contract, and whether the department may proceed with the caterer as insured.
answers.answer: The minimum general liability limits in the UC Terms and Conditions do not vary with the value of the contract. The required Commercial Form General Liability Insurance must have a per-occurrence limit of $1,000,000 [2]. Therefore, the department may not proceed with the caterer as insured, as the caterer’s policy does not meet the minimum requirement [2].
cited: UC Terms and Conditions of Purchase (April 2025) p.8

answers.subject: Protected health information; institutional data; applicable appendices
answers.input: A vendor will analyze de-identified patient records for a research study and, in the course of the engagement, will also be given access to the department's internal file server, which holds administrative records. Whether a Business Associate Agreement is required; whether the Appendix - Data Security is required; and whether both may apply to a single engagement.
answers.answer: A Business Associate Agreement (BAA) is not required for this engagement because the vendor is not directly handling protected health information (PHI) but rather de-identified patient records, which are not considered PHI under HIPAA [5]. However, the Appendix - Data Security is required because the vendor will have access to Institutional Information, including administrative records, which are subject to the data security requirements outlined in the Appendix [1][6]. Both the Appendix - Data Security and a BAA may apply to a single engagement if the vendor also handles PHI, but in this case, only the Appendix - Data Security applies [5][6].
cited: Appendix: Data Security Requirements p.2
BFB-IS-3: Electronic Information Security p.32
Appendix: Data Security Requirements p.1

answers.subject: Worker classification; recently separated employee
answers.input: A department proposes to pay an employee who separated from the University last month as an independent contractor to perform the same duties, on the same schedule, using University equipment and workspace. Whether the worker may be classified as an independent contractor under the Internal Revenue Service common law standards summarized in the Guidelines, and what the consequence of misclassification is.
answers.answer:
Under the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) common law standards summarized in the UC Independent Contractor Guidelines, the worker may not be classified as an independent contractor if the individual is an employee who has separated from the University. The IRS generally considers the relationship between the worker and the University, including the degree of control the University exercises over the worker's activities, the method of payment, and whether the worker is engaged in an ongoing relationship with the University. 

If the worker is an ex-employee who is now being paid as an independent contractor to perform the same duties, on the same schedule, using University equipment and workspace, the University may be misclassifying the worker as an independent contractor. The IRS typically views such arrangements as continuing employment relationships, especially when the work is similar to the worker's previous employment and the University maintains control over the work. This misclassification could result in significant tax liabilities for the University, including back taxes, penalties, and interest. [3], [7]
cited: UC Independent Contractor Guidelines p.10
UC Independent Contractor Guidelines p.10

answers.subject: Employee gifts; per-person limit
answers.input: A department proposes to give a $150 gift card to each of five employees in recognition of the completion of a project. Whether the proposed gifts exceed the per-person limit for employee recognition awards, and what the tax treatment is if the limit is exceeded.
answers.answer:
The proposed gifts of $150 gift cards to each of five employees exceed the per-person limit for employee recognition awards. The per-person limit for employee recognition awards is $75 [4]. Therefore, each $150 gift card exceeds this limit by $75.

If the limit is exceeded, the tax treatment is that the entire amount of the gift is taxable to the employee. This is because the IRS treats the value of the gift as taxable income when it exceeds the de minimis limit [7]. Specifically, if the value of the award exceeds the $75 de minimis limit, the entire amount is taxable [7]. 

Additionally, gift cards of any value provided for a length of service or safety award are not considered tangible personal property and are subject to withholding as wage income [5]. While this specific reference is for length of service awards, the principle that gift cards are treated as taxable income if they exceed the limit applies here as well.
cited: BFB-G-41: Employee Non-Cash Awards & Gifts p.2

answers.subject: Moving and relocation; current employee transferring between locations
answers.input: A current employee in a Professional and Support Staff position transfers from another University location to UC Santa Cruz. The hiring department states that moving expense reimbursement is available only to newly hired employees. Whether a current employee who transfers to a new University location is eligible for reimbursement of moving expenses under G-13.
answers.answer: A current employee who transfers to a new University location is eligible for reimbursement of moving expenses under G-13, provided the move is closely related to the start of work and meets both the time and distance tests under I.R.C. Section 217(c). The University may reimburse the employee or pay a third party on behalf of the employee for moving expenses if the move is made in connection with the commencement of work at a new job location and the moving expenses are incurred within one year from the time the employee first reports to the new job [1]. Additionally, during the 12-month period immediately following the move, the individual must be employed full-time for at least 39 weeks [4]. The policy explicitly states that moving expenses may be paid by the University when a current employee is required to transfer or accepts a position, including a position at the same grade or a lower grade, at a campus outside a reasonable commuting distance [1]. Therefore, the hiring department's statement that reimbursement is only available to newly hired employees is inconsistent with the policy.
cited: BFB-G-13: Moving & Relocation Policy p.3
BFB-G-13: Moving & Relocation Policy p.3

answers.subject: Federal contract funds; FAR Part 12 commercial items
answers.input: A department proposes to purchase commercial off-the-shelf software with funds from a federal contract. It asks which Federal Acquisition Regulation Part 12 (commercial items) requirements must be flowed down to the supplier. Whether University policy or the UC Terms and Conditions specify FAR Part 12 requirements for purchases under federal contracts, or whether the applicable clauses are to be determined from the prime contract. If the question is not addressed by policy, please so state.
answers.answer: The UC Terms and Conditions of Purchase (April 2025) specify that for transactions involving funds on a federal grant or cooperative agreement, the applicable provisions of the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) are flowed down to the supplier [4]. Specifically, for commercial items, the requirements of FAR Part 12 (commercial items) are incorporated into the terms and conditions of purchase, and therefore must be flowed down to the supplier. This is consistent with the UC policy that requires compliance with FAR and DFARS requirements when using funds from federal grants and contracts [6]. Thus, the applicable clauses are determined by the prime contract and the UC Terms and Conditions of Purchase, which incorporate FAR Part 12 requirements for commercial items.
cited: UC Terms and Conditions of Purchase (April 2025) p.7
BFB-BUS-43: Procurement & Supply Chain Management (Interim, Jan 2026) p.13

answers.subject: Use of another public agency's competitively awarded contract
answers.input: A department proposes to purchase fleet vehicles through a contract competitively awarded by another California public agency, under a cooperative purchasing provision in that contract, rather than through a University solicitation. Whether BUS-43 permits the University to rely on another public agency's competitive award in lieu of its own solicitation, and under what conditions. If the question is not addressed by policy, please so state.
answers.answer: The University may rely on another public agency's competitive award in lieu of its own solicitation under certain conditions. Specifically, the University is permitted to use cooperative purchasing provisions from another California public agency, provided that the terms and conditions of the award meet the requirements of the California Public Contract Code and the University's procurement policies. This is consistent with the basis of Presidential Policy BUS-43, which is grounded in the California Public Contract Code, Part 2, Contracting by State Agencies, Chapter 2.1, University of California Competitive Bidding, Article 2, Materials, Goods, and Services (Public Contract Code Section 10507, et seq.) [5]. Additionally, the University must ensure that the cooperative purchasing arrangement is coordinated with the Vehicle Commodity Manager, particularly if the transaction involves special purpose vehicles or alternative fuel vehicles [7]. The use of such arrangements must also comply with the general use vehicle procurement provisions outlined in UCPS-120029 [7].
cited: BFB-BUS-43: Procurement & Supply Chain Management (Interim, Jan 2026) p.2
UCPS-120029: Acquisition & Disposition of University Vehicles p.5

answers.subject: SSPR processing time
answers.input: A department submits an SSPR form for a $75,000 purchase funded by a federal grant and asks how many business days Procurement Services requires to review it. Whether University policy prescribes a time within which an SSPR must be reviewed. If the question is a matter of office practice rather than policy, please so state and indicate the current practice.
answers.answer:
Answer: No, University policy does not prescribe a specific number of business days within which an SSPR must be reviewed.
Rule: Competitive bid required: NO ($75,000; threshold $100,000). SSPR required: YES (threshold $50,000; sections I, II, VII, VIII). Also required: Federal Funds Checklist; Debarment & Suspension Verification; Uniform Guidance (2 CFR 200) Flow-Down Articles.
